newsitem.title: JAPAN: S&P assigns "BBB" PI rating to five Japanese banks.
newsitem.headline: S&P assigns "BBB" PI rating to five Japanese banks.

text.p: Standard & Poor's (S&P) said on Tuesday it had assigned "BBB" public information ratings to five regional Japanese banks.
The rating agency also said that it had assigned public information ratings of "A" and "BB" to two other regional banks.
The public information ratings were recently introduced by S&P.
The ratings are as follows:
Hachijuni Bank Ltd Api
Bank of Yokohama Ltd BBBpi
Hyakujushi Bank Ltd BBBpi
Iyo Bank Ltd BBBpi
Nanto Bank Ltd BBBpi
Suruga Bank Ltd BBBpi
Kiyo Bank Ltd BBpi

"Despite the prolonged financial stress that has affected the Japanese banking industry overall, most Tier 1 regional banks have maintained healthy profiles supported by broad-based lending, relatively sound asset quality, and satisfactory capitalisation along with core profitability," Standard & Poor's said in a statement.
The "pi" subscript following the rating shows capital market participants that the ratings are based on public information, the statement said.
Before assigning "pi" ratings, the firm contacted the banks, notified them of its plans, and provided an opportunity to meet analysts, the statement said.
"Tier 1 (regional) banks benefit from dominant market positions in their respective prefectures," S&P said.

"The well-balanced industrial bases of the prefectures alleviate economic cyclicality, while the banks also enjoy strong liquidity backed by prefecture-wide retail networks and customers' high deposit ratios," it added.

The banks' relatively sound asset quality has been helped by low exposure to high-risk areas like construction, real estate and non-bank sectors, where Japan's top 20 banks rapidly expanded credit in the late 1980s, S&P said.
But S&P warned that some Tier 1 regional banks have been severely hit by problem loans, noting that nine out of 64 banks posted net losses due to huge write-offs in 1995/96.

"Some banks extended high-risk loans to the real estate and non-bank sectors which, along with volatility in land prices, have contributed to a widening credit-quality gap among regional banks," the agency said.
But it added that the credit quality of these banks was partly mitigated by healthy loan portfolios, and that their problem loans were manageable in terms of capital and profits.
S&P said the solid standing of Tier 1 regional banks will not change dramatically because of their comparatively healthy profiles and strong ties with local customers.
"Nevertheless, those banks which are burdened by asset-quality problems and a deteriorated risk-absorption capacity will be hard pressed to maintain their competitive positions," it said.

The agency said its new ratings are distinguished from its full debt ratings, which involve confidential information and lengthy consultations with the issuer, by a "pi" attached to the familiar letter grade.
The move follows S&P's announcement last month that it would expand its worldwide bank coverage by assigning ratings based on public information.
S&P said it plans to assign about 250 new bank ratings, mostly in emerging markets, over the next few months.
